summary: Gives explicit inequalities and detailed criteria for evaluating neighbors as loop-free alternates for multi-homed prefixes, improving on earlier implementation experience.

eli5.summary: When a road closes, you need a backup route that does not lead back. This gives math rules for choosing safe backups.

subtitle: Explicit inequalities for picking backup next hops when a prefix is announced by more than one router.

tldr.problem: A router that wants a pre-computed backup path (a loop-free alternate) for a prefix announced by several routers had only a loosely worded method in RFC 5286, and deployment experience showed gaps for OSPF external prefixes, IS-IS default routes, MAX_METRIC links and multi-topology networks.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC gives explicit inequalities for link-protecting, downstream-paths-only and node-protecting alternates, adds step-by-step rules for choosing alternate OSPF ASBRs, and clarifies how to treat IS-IS ATT-bit default routes, MAX_METRIC links and multi-topology deployments.
tldr.outcome: It updates Section 6 of RFC 5286 and gives the same results as the earlier method for multi-homed prefixes, with better coverage in some ECMP cases. It is a Proposed Standard and nothing has obsoleted it.

today: RFC 8518 is a Proposed Standard from March 2019 that updates RFC 5286, and nothing has obsoleted or updated it.

sections.title: Multi-Homed Prefixes and Loop-Free Alternates
sections.content:
IP Fast Reroute (FRR) lets a router prepare a backup next hop before a failure happens. RFC 5286 specifies the use of loop-free alternates (LFAs) for this. When a prefix is advertised by more than one router it is called a multi-homed prefix (MHP). MHPs arise for prefixes learned from outside the routing domain by several routers, for subnets announced from both ends of a link, and for prefixes advertised by several routers for resiliency.

Section 6.1 of RFC 5286 describes a method for finding LFAs for MHPs. This document restates it with explicit inequalities that give equivalent results, and it gives detailed criteria for external prefixes advertised by OSPF ASBRs. It also adds clarifications on three observations from operation: the IS-IS ATT (attach) bit in a Level 1 area, links provisioned with MAX_METRIC for traffic engineering, and multi-topology IGP deployments.

The RFC reuses the terminology of RFC 5714 and the inequality notation of RFC 5286.
sections.eli5: Some places can be reached through more than one door. This RFC explains how a router picks a safe backup path to such a place before any road breaks.

sections.title: The LFA Inequalities for Multi-Homed Prefixes
sections.content:
The inequalities use D_opt(X,Y), the metric sum of the shortest path from X to Y, and Cost(X,Y), the metric of prefix Y as announced by the prefix-originating node X. They follow from the inequalities of RFC 5286 combined with the observation that D_opt(N,P) = Min (D_opt(N,PO_i) + Cost(PO_i,P)) over all originators PO_i.

The notation is: P is the prefix being evaluated, S the computing router, N the neighbor being evaluated as an alternate, E the primary next hop on the shortest path from S to P, PO_i the originator being evaluated and PO_best the originator on the shortest path from S to P.

Three kinds of alternate are defined:

  • Link-protecting: N is an LFA if and only if the first inequality holds.
  • Link-protecting plus downstream-paths-only: a stricter condition that applies to more complex failure scenarios.
  • Node-protecting: N must be loop-free with respect to both E and P, so its path to P must not go through E.
sections.eli5: A router asks, for each neighbor, whether that neighbor's own way to the destination is shorter than the trip back through the router. If it is, the neighbor will not send traffic straight back.

sections.title: Selecting LFAs for Multi-Homed Prefixes
sections.content:
To compute a valid LFA for an MHP, the computing router S MUST, for each alternate neighbor N, follow the matching procedure once for each remote node that originated the prefix.

If N is itself an originator of the prefix, it cannot loop packets for that prefix back to S. N MUST then be chosen as a valid LFA without evaluating the inequalities, as long as a downstream-paths-only LFA is not desired. To make sure such a neighbor also gives a downstream-paths-only LFA, S MUST also evaluate that inequality for N.

If N is not an originator, S MUST evaluate the corresponding inequality from Section 2. If N satisfies it, S MUST choose N as one of the valid LFAs for the prefix. More specific rules for external prefixes are in Section 4 of the RFC.
sections.eli5: If your neighbor already lives at the destination, it is a safe backup right away. Otherwise you check it with the math rule first.

sections.title: Better Coverage With the Simplified Approach
sections.content:
RFC 5286 lets a router simplify the MHP calculation by assuming the prefix is attached only to the router that was its pre-failure optimal point of attachment, at the expense of potentially lower coverage. This RFC notes that its procedure can improve coverage for ECMP MHPs in that case without extra computational cost.

In the first example network, prefix P is advertised from both E and F, which share the same primary next hop. The simplified approach would give P only a link-protecting LFA through neighbor C, while neighbor A offers node protection. An implementation MAY compare the protection A gives to F with the protection C gives to E and inherit the better one, which here is A.

In the second example, P is reachable at cost 20 through both E and F, but the primary next hop to each is different. In that case P MUST inherit the LFAs calculated for each primary next hop, which are nodes N1 and N2 respectively.
sections.eli5: If two doors share the same hallway, you can pick whichever backup is safest. If they use different hallways, each hallway keeps its own backup.

sections.title: IS-IS Default Routes and the ATT Bit
sections.content:
Under RFC 1195, a Level 1 router adds a default route to the closest reachable Level 1/Level 2 router that advertises the ATT (attach) bit in its LSP-0 fragment. The base LFA specification gives no procedure for computing an LFA for such a default route.

This RFC specifies that a node can treat the default route as advertised by the border L1/L2 router where the ATT bit is set, and compute LFAs for it. When several ECMP L1/L2 routers are reachable, the best LFAs SHOULD be computed for each primary next hop of the default route, as in the ECMP MHP example above. The RFC states that it does not alter ECMP handling rules or the computation of LFAs for ECMP in general.
sections.eli5: A default route is the path you take when you do not know where something is. This RFC lets a router prepare a backup for that path too.

sections.title: Multi-Homed External Prefixes and Alternate ASBRs
sections.content:
External routes are redistributed into an IGP, for example when two networks merge or during protocol migrations. When no LFA exists for the best ASBR, it can help to consider the other ASBRs that redistribute the same routes as alternates.

For IS-IS, evaluation of multi-homed external prefixes is the same as for internal ones, and the Section 2 inequalities apply. For OSPF, extra rules are needed because of the external route calculation in RFC 2328. When a primary ASBR has been chosen and another ASBR originates the same prefix, the alternate is screened in order:

  • If RFC1583Compatibility is disabled, the paths must be intra-area non-backbone, or intra-area backbone and/or inter-area, otherwise the alternate is skipped.
  • The cost types (type 1 or type 2) of the two ASBRs must match, otherwise the alternate is skipped.
  • Equal type 1 costs give ECMP FRR. For type 2, different costs mean the alternate is skipped; equal costs with equal cost to reach the ASBR or forwarding address give ECMP FRR.
  • The route types (type 5 and type 7) must match, and for type 7 the p-bit and forwarding address must match.
  • Only then is the inequality applied to the alternate ASBR.

The inequalities for external prefixes mirror those in Section 2. When the forwarding address is non-zero, they use F_opt(X,Y), the distance from X to the forwarding address specified by ASBR Y. For ASBRs advertising type 1 and type 2 costs, they use the same D_opt form as Section 2, with Cost(X,Y) meaning the external cost.
sections.eli5: When the same outside address can be reached through several gateways, the router first throws out gateways that play by different rules. Then it checks the leftover ones with the math rule.

sections.title: MAX_METRIC Links and Multi-Topology Networks
sections.content:
RFC 5286 excludes nodes and links from alternate paths based on the maximum link metric, called MAX_METRIC (0xffffff or 2^24 - 1 for IS-IS, 0xffff for OSPF). Followed strictly, this can discard the only neighbor that satisfies the basic loop-free condition. In the example, a link has cost 10 forward but MAX_METRIC in reverse for a traffic engineering requirement, yet primary traffic still uses that link. The RFC says the link MAY be used as an LFA anyway. Alternatively, the reverse metric MAY be configured as MAX_METRIC-1 so the link stays usable without updating the router.

RFC 5286 called multi-topology OSPF and IS-IS out of scope. This RFC clarifies that in multi-topology deployments a separate shortest path tree is built per MT-ID, so the LFA principles apply, and the eligible neighbor set is determined per MT-ID by the presence of an IGP adjacency on that MT-ID. For MT IS-IS with the standard unicast topology (MT-ID #0) carrying both IPv4 and IPv6, network congruency applies: the same address families must be provisioned on all links and nodes.
sections.eli5: A road marked as very expensive in one direction may still be fine as a backup. And when a city has separate maps for different traffic types, each map gets its own list of backups.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The existing OSPF security considerations continue to apply, as do the recommended manual key management mechanisms in RFC 7474. The existing IS-IS security considerations also continue to apply, as given in RFC 5304 and RFC 5310 and extended by RFC 7645 for KARP.

The document does not change any of the protocol specifications it discusses, so the security considerations of RFC 5286 continue to apply. It has no IANA actions.
sections.eli5: This RFC only changes how a router picks backups, not how routers talk, so the old safety rules still cover it.
